lead: A psychrometric chart, also called a humidity chart, puts every property of moist air on one sheet. Dry-bulb temperature runs along the bottom and humidity up the side. Any two independent readings fix a point, and the rest — dew point, relative humidity, wet-bulb temperature, enthalpy, humid volume — are read from lines through that point. It exists to save repeated calculations in drying, cooling towers and air conditioning. The standard chart is drawn for air–water at 1 atm.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.1 for dry-bulb temperature, absolute humidity, relative humidity and dew point.

blocks.text: The horizontal axis is dry-bulb temperature T in °C. The vertical axis is humidity Y in kg water vapour per kg dry air. A point on the sheet is one state of moist air. The saturation curve is the 100% relative-humidity line; below it air is unsaturated, and above it the mixture would be fog.

Curves of constant relative humidity run below the saturation curve. A horizontal line is constant Y. Its left end meets the saturation curve at the dew point, because cooling at constant Y raises relative humidity until condensation starts. The wet-bulb temperature is the steady reading of a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in a wet wick in moving air; Chapter 7.3 shows that for air–water it equals the adiabatic saturation temperature. Wet-bulb lines start on the saturation curve and slope down to the right. Enthalpy lines lie nearly parallel to them; the reason is in Chapter 7.3. Humid-volume lines give volume per kg dry air.

blocks.where: h is moist-air enthalpy in kJ/kg dry air; T is dry-bulb temperature in °C; Y is humidity in kg water/kg dry air. The constants 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), 2500 kJ/kg and 1.88 kJ/(kg·K) are the dry-air specific heat, the latent heat of water at 0 °C and the water-vapour specific heat.

blocks.text: One chart is valid for one total pressure, usually 1 atm, and for air–water only. At another pressure the same Y gives a different water-vapour partial pressure, so every curve shifts. Check the pressure printed on the chart.

sections.h3: Fixing a state and following a process

items: Start with two independent readings: usually dry-bulb plus wet-bulb, or dry-bulb plus dew point.
For dry-bulb plus wet-bulb, intersect the vertical dry-bulb line with the sloping wet-bulb line marked with that temperature.
For dry-bulb plus dew point, find the dew point on the saturation curve. Run a horizontal from there to the dry-bulb vertical.

From the point, read Y on the y-axis, dew point along the horizontal to saturation, relative humidity from the nearest curve, enthalpy from the sloping enthalpy scale through the point (close to the wet-bulb line but not the same line), and humid volume from its own line.

blocks.text: Processes are paths. Heating is horizontal to the right: Y stays fixed, so no water is added or removed. Cooling is horizontal to the left until the saturation curve. Further cooling follows the saturation curve and water condenses. Humidification with recirculated water runs up an adiabatic line, as Chapter 7.4 shows.
Do not read enthalpy by moving horizontally. A horizontal move changes only sensible heat; the chart's enthalpy lines are the sloping ones.

sections.h3: Mixing two streams: the lever rule

blocks.text: Two air streams that mix without heat or work loss give a point on the straight line joining their states. Use dry-air mass flows, not moist-air flows. For stream A with dry-air flow m<sub>A</sub> and stream B with m<sub>B</sub>, the mixture humidity and enthalpy are weighted averages.

blocks.where: Y<sub>mix</sub> is mixture humidity; Y<sub>A</sub> and Y<sub>B</sub> are stream humidities; m<sub>A</sub> and m<sub>B</sub> are dry-air mass flows, all in consistent units. Enthalpy uses the same weights: h<sub>mix</sub> = (m<sub>A</sub> h<sub>A</sub> + m<sub>B</sub> h<sub>B</sub>)/(m<sub>A</sub> + m<sub>B</sub>).

blocks.text: The point divides the line in inverse proportion to the dry-air flows. If m<sub>A</sub> is larger, the mixture lies nearer A. Distance from A to the mixture divided by distance from A to B equals m<sub>B</sub>/(m<sub>A</sub>+m<sub>B</sub>). Once Y<sub>mix</sub> and h<sub>mix</sub> are known, the mixture temperature follows from the enthalpy formula or is read from the chart.
In the worked example, 100 kg dry air/h at 30 °C and Y = 0.010 mixes with 50 kg dry air/h at 40 °C and Y = 0.020. The mixture is one-third of the way from A to B.

figure.caption: The worked example on a 1 atm chart. Stream A (100 kg dry air/h at 30 °C, Y = 0.010) and stream B (50 kg/h at 40 °C, Y = 0.020) mix to Y = 0.0133 and h = 67.7 kJ/kg dry air, which puts the mixture at 33.4 °C on the straight line AB, one-third of the way from A because A is the larger stream. Dashed curves are 20, 40, 60 and 80 % RH.

spec.aria: Psychrometric chart from 20 to 45 degrees with the saturation curve and relative humidity curves. Points A at 30 degrees and B at 40 degrees are joined by a straight line; the mixture point at 33.4 degrees lies one third of the way from A.

examples.question: At 1 atm, 100 kg dry air/h at 30 °C with humidity 0.010 kg/kg dry air mixes with 50 kg dry air/h at 40 °C with humidity 0.020 kg/kg dry air. Find the mixture humidity, enthalpy and dry-bulb temperature. Check the position by the lever rule.
steps: Basis: m<sub>A</sub> = 100 kg dry air/h, T<sub>A</sub> = 30 °C, Y<sub>A</sub> = 0.010 kg/kg dry air; m<sub>B</sub> = 50 kg dry air/h, T<sub>B</sub> = 40 °C, Y<sub>B</sub> = 0.020 kg/kg dry air; total m = 150 kg dry air/h.
The distance from A is m<sub>B</sub>/(m<sub>A</sub>+m<sub>B</sub>) = 50/150 = 1/3 of AB, so the mixture is closer to A, consistent with the plotted point.
examples.answer: Y<sub>mix</sub> = 0.0133 kg/kg dry air, h<sub>mix</sub> = 67.7 kJ/kg dry air, T<sub>mix</sub> = 33.4 °C; the point lies one-third of the way from stream A to stream B.
examples.check:
m<sub>A</sub> = 100.0
Y<sub>A</sub> = 0.010
T<sub>A</sub> = 30.0
m<sub>B</sub> = 50.0
Y<sub>B</sub> = 0.020
T<sub>B</sub> = 40.0
m = m<sub>A</sub> + m<sub>B</sub>
Y<sub>mix</sub> = (m<sub>A</sub>*Y<sub>A</sub> + m<sub>B</sub>*Y<sub>B</sub>)/m
h<sub>A</sub> = 1.005*T<sub>A</sub> + Y<sub>A</sub>*(2500 + 1.88*T<sub>A</sub>)
h<sub>B</sub> = 1.005*T<sub>B</sub> + Y<sub>B</sub>*(2500 + 1.88*T<sub>B</sub>)
h<sub>mix</sub> = (m<sub>A</sub>*h<sub>A</sub> + m<sub>B</sub>*h<sub>B</sub>)/m
T<sub>mix</sub> = (h<sub>mix</sub> - 2500*Y<sub>mix</sub>)/(1.005 + 1.88*Y<sub>mix</sub>)
print(f"{Y<sub>mix</sub>:.4f}")
print(f"{h<sub>A</sub>:.1f}")
print(f"{h<sub>B</sub>:.1f}")
print(f"{h<sub>mix</sub>:.1f}")
print(f"{T<sub>mix</sub>:.1f}")

traps: Using a 1 atm chart for air at 2 atm or for a vacuum dryer. Y, relative humidity and wet-bulb lines all change with total pressure.
Reading enthalpy along a horizontal line. Enthalpy lines are the sloping lines nearly parallel to the wet-bulb lines.
Confusing wet-bulb temperature with dew point. They are equal only at saturation; in unsaturated air the wet-bulb is higher.
Mixing with moist-air mass flows. The lever rule and Y balance use dry-air flows; moist-air flow includes the water vapour.
Cooling below the dew point by a horizontal path. Once saturation is reached the path bends along the saturation curve and liquid water leaves the air.

quiz.q: On a psychrometric chart, what is plotted on the horizontal and vertical axes?
quiz.a: Dry-bulb temperature in °C horizontally and humidity Y in kg water/kg dry air vertically.

quiz.q: Which line on the chart represents saturated air?
quiz.a: The saturation curve, the 100% relative-humidity line.

quiz.q: Why does the dew point lie on a horizontal line from a state point?
quiz.a: A horizontal line has constant Y, hence constant water-vapour partial pressure. Cooling at constant Y reaches saturation at the dew point, so the left end of that horizontal is the dew point.

quiz.q: Why is one chart not valid for all total pressures?
quiz.a: Humidity, relative humidity and dew point depend on the water-vapour partial pressure, which is set by total pressure at a given Y. Changing total pressure moves the saturation and relative-humidity curves.

quiz.q: Air at 30 °C dry-bulb and 20 °C dew point at 1 atm. How do you locate the state, and what is Y approximately?
quiz.a: At 20 °C on the saturation curve, Y ≈ 0.0147 kg/kg. Draw the horizontal at this Y to the 30 °C vertical; that intersection is the state. Read relative humidity near 55%.

quiz.q: 1 kg dry air/s at 25 °C and Y = 0.008 is heated to 40 °C at constant Y. Find the heat added.
Two streams mix: 300 kg dry air/h at state A and 100 kg dry air/h at state B. Where is the mixture on the chart line?
quiz.a: On line AB, at distance from A equal to 100/(300+100) = 1/4 of AB, so closer to A.

quiz.q: Air at 35 °C and Y = 0.020 is cooled to 15 °C at 1 atm. Describe the path.
quiz.a: Cool horizontally at constant Y until the saturation curve, at the dew point near 25 °C, then follow the saturation curve to 15 °C. Water condenses after saturation; the final air is saturated at 15 °C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Psychrometric charts are built into HVAC selection software and dryer design spreadsheets, and the same equations generate charts for any total pressure or gas–vapour pair. Research on evaporative cooling and drying uses the chart to set inlet air states and to find the limiting wet-bulb temperature. Modern curricula often add computer plotting of the saturation and enthalpy lines. Search for 'psychrometric chart 1 atm', 'air water humidity chart' or 'wet bulb enthalpy chart' to see worked charts.
